# Heavy Truck OBD2 vs. Car OBD2: Why Your Interface Works on a Caddy but Not a MAN

You have verified the basics: the voltage difference between a standard 12V automotive bus and a heavy-duty 24V system is known, and you are correctly isolating the CAN-High and CAN-Low pins from the wider OBD-II connector. You've confirmed that your Arduino with a CAN-bus shield can communicate successfully with a VW Caddy using specific UDS requests. Theoretically, if the protocol is standardized, the same payload should work on a MAN or Mercedes truck. If it doesn't, the issue isn't necessarily the voltage or the physical layer; it's almost certainly the communication protocol and the specific implementation of the ISO 15765-4 stack found in heavy-duty vehicles.

The root cause lies in how Universal Diagnostic Services (UDS) are wrapped in CAN frames. In a standard passenger car, you often encounter two distinct modes: the "Low Speed" mode and the "High Speed" mode. The Low Speed mode typically runs at 500 kbps using short Identifiers (11-bit). This is likely what your Caddy is responding to when you send `t7DF80201000000000000`. However, heavy-duty trucks frequently default to or require the High Speed mode, which runs at 1 Mbps using Extended Identifiers (29-bit).

When you attempt to read from a truck using an 11-bit identifier like `7DF`, you are technically speaking the wrong dialect. Even if the truck supports UDS over CAN, it may be listening exclusively on the extended ID space for production traffic, ignoring short IDs entirely. Switching to the extended form, such as `e18DB33F18020100ffffffffff`, addresses this mismatch. The `E` prefix indicates an extended frame, and the identifier `18DB33F18` is the specific address often reserved for UDS services in High Speed mode. If your truck hardware is configured for High Speed operation but your interface sends Low Speed frames (or vice versa), the controller will simply ignore the traffic as if it were noise on the bus.

The speed setting you are testingâ250 kbps, 500 kbps, and 1000 kbpsâis another critical variable. Many heavy-duty vehicles operate their CAN bus at a fixed 500 kbps in High Speed mode or require a specific initialization sequence to switch modes. Some trucks do not allow dynamic switching from Low to High speed on the fly; they expect the node to match the bus configuration immediately upon connection. If your ELM327-based device or your Arduino shield is hardcoded to initialize at 500 kbps while the truck expects 1 Mbps (or vice versa) before any diagnostic session starts, communication will fail regardless of the payload content.

Furthermore, you must consider the specific UDS transport layer implementation. While ISO 15031 defines the service definitions (like `02` for read data by identifier), the exact byte stuffing, frame delimiters, and error handling can vary between manufacturers. Some OEMs implement proprietary extensions to the standard UDS protocol or require a specific Security Access session before allowing access to certain PIDs. You might be hitting a response timeout because the truck expects a different physical layer negotiation sequence that your current interface doesn't trigger.

Before concluding that the protocols are fundamentally different, verify the exact bus speed and identifier type supported by the specific truck model via the manufacturer's service documentation. Often, the solution is simply switching your diagnostic tool from Short ID/Low Speed mode to Extended ID/High Speed mode and ensuring the baud rate matches the hardware configuration of the 24V system. If the truck utilizes a different physical layer entirely, such as FlexRay or proprietary CAN variants, standard OBD-II interfaces will not suffice without specific gateway adapters designed for that chassis architecture.
